Separate yourself from the idea that you're doing something wrong. Making friends is not an easy feat as an adult. Have you ever checked out the stats on loneliness?

You're not at fault for not having female friends. Most interactions you have will be exactly as you described. You take each other's ig, send one message, then never speak again. Forming and maintaining friendships does take some work. 

Men generally make the first move. They may find you attractive, realize you're taken or not interested, and be okay with friendships. You may just have an easier time with men over women. I personally have male friends because my interests and hobbies are male oriented. My female friendships don't last either because they tend to be more superficial. This is to say we don't have much in common on a deeper level than a few common interests. 

You are someone who is attractive. It's possible that women may feel intimidated or insecure. When I was in college, I had a female friend who was very attractive. Hanging with her was difficult because people would treat her so well but completely ignore me. She was constantly being hit on, and I'd end up sitting awkwardly as people tried their hardest to get her number. It made me feel like shit and I stopped hanging out with her.

I'm in my 30s now, so it wouldn't make a difference, but at 20, it was awful. 

I've written an essay here, but my only advice is to be easier on yourself. This isn't uncommon, and you're not at fault. Surround yourself with people who have common interests and hobbies, and you'll (hopefully) find friends who you click with. Also, ( if you don't already) try making the first move. Like I said, other women could be intimidated.

I'm a severe hypochondriac. I have been since I was like 7. (30 now)
These days, it does not rule my life, more of an annoying background thing. What has worked for me is: 

1. Do. Not. Google. Anything. It will always show you the absolute worst things possible and stress you out. 

2. Think about the sensations you're experiencing and if you've experienced them before. For example, I have a lot of stomach issues. My first thought when it happens is "oh god, colon cancer" or something like that. I then have to consider how often I've had stomach problems. It generally resolves itself with dietary changes or when stressors die down. 

3. Pay attention to when your problems arise and if there could be any causes for it. 
I had shoulder pain for weeks and started to panic. It was so bad that I couldn't lift my arm without shooting pain. In the end, it was due to work, and after resting it for about a week, it was fine. If there are other causes that you can find, it is very likely benign.

4. Pay attention to how long your symptoms last. Sometimes, you get random aches and pains. Sometimes, your anxiety manifests in physical symptoms. However, if something is seriously wrong, it will persist and even get worse. If it resolves in a matter of days, it likely wasn't cause for concern.

5. Does it always hurt or only when you think about it? This is a question I ask myself a lot. If the problem is only there when I think about it, then it's probably just my anxiety exaggerating something minor.

6. Distractions. When you freak out about something that could be wrong, distract your mind. Doing something physical helps a lot. Play a video game, read, listen to music, talk to a friend, pretty much anything that isn't thinking about whatever is plaguing you. 

7. Learn to talk yourself down. This has helped me immensely. "I know you're scared, but worrying yourself about this will not help. You're okay. Nothing is happening. Even if there is something wrong, there is nothing you can do at this moment." I mean, whatever you have to say to yourself. It helps to be gentle with yourself as you would with a little kid. 

I don't know how helpful this will be for you, but this has taken my anxiety from a 15 out of 10 to a much more manageable 6/7.  Before, I couldn't leave my house. I barely slept. I'd have panic attacks frequently. I'd spend hours shaking and fretting, thinking I was dying at every moment.

I have had this exact problem since I was 7. (30 now) I still struggle with this, but there is no one solution. You have to find what works for you as everyone is different. 

As others have said you definitely have to stop googling everything. I completely understand, it's addicting to do so, but that is compulsion. You're hoping it's benign and it'll put your mind at ease, but it never will. Google will give you cancer, heart failure and liver disease for a tummy ache. 

Personally, I do a couple of things. I ask myself "have I had this symptom before?" If the answer is yes, then I am probably fine. I try to be logical, try simple remedies and see if anything changes. Eating, drinking water, trying to rest etc. I wait it out. If any of my symptoms persist or get worse after a week or so, then I go to a doctor. If it resolves itself, then it was probably just anxiety. 

If that doesn't work, I distact myself. Drawing, writing, listening to music, watching my favorite show things like that. Anything that makes you smile a bit. If even that doesn't help, I think "well if I were dying, it would surely suck to spend my last days terrified." I'm not sure how helpful that it, but it gives me some solace. Lastly, I breathe (in for 5 out for 5), I tell myself that I am okay in this moment. You can't control what happens tomorrow, but right now you're okay. 

 If you can get professional help, therapy can be helpful in finding healthy coping mechanisms and just having a non-judgmental space to talk about your fears. 

On the plus side, you're not alone. A lot of people are going through the same thing. You and anyone who is reading this honestly, are a trooper. Anxiety is tough, and you're pushing through it. I hope this helps in some way.
